Section 1

Abstract

This project explores Kerberoasting, a post-exploitation attack technique that allows any authenticated domain user to request Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for service accounts with registered Service Principal Names (SPNs), and subsequently attempt offline password cracking against those tickets. The attack requires no special privileges and exploits a fundamental design characteristic of the Kerberos protocol.

This educational project develops an isolated Windows Server 2022 Active Directory lab environment using synthetic identities to document the attack surface, implement Group Policy Object (GPO) hardening, configure advanced audit policies, and deploy Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) to eliminate the primary attack vector. A companion Python Flask web application provides an interactive dashboard for risk scenario review, defensive control scoring, and automated risk assessment.

All work is performed exclusively in an offline, isolated virtual environment. No production systems, real credentials, or live networks are used at any stage.

Section 2

Problem Statement

Kerberoasting has been documented as one of the most reliably effective Active Directory attack techniques since its public disclosure in 2014. It remains prevalent because:

  • The Kerberos protocol requires no special permissions to request a TGS ticket for any registered SPN
  • Many organisations maintain service accounts with static, human-memorable passwords set years ago
  • RC4-HMAC encryption (0x17) — the default in legacy domains — produces tickets susceptible to fast offline cracking
  • Without proper audit logging, TGS enumeration for multiple SPNs is invisible in event logs
  • Service accounts frequently hold excess privileges, converting a cracked password into a domain compromise

The consequences of a successful Kerberoasting attack range from service account compromise through lateral movement to full domain takeover when privileged accounts are targeted. Despite being well-understood, many enterprise environments lack the basic controls needed to detect or prevent it.

Section 3

Objectives

  1. Build an isolated Windows Server 2022 Active Directory lab with synthetic service accounts and SPNs
  2. Document and understand the Kerberoasting attack vector from a defender's perspective
  3. Implement and verify AES-only Kerberos encryption enforcement via GPO
  4. Deploy Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) to eliminate static passwords on SPN accounts
  5. Configure Advanced Audit Policies to capture Event ID 4769 for detection
  6. Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging to detect tool-based enumeration
  7. Apply least-privilege principles and Protected Users group to Tier-0 accounts
  8. Develop an interactive Flask application for risk assessment and control scoring
  9. Produce verifiable evidence of defensive controls for academic submission

Section 5

Methodology

5.1 Research Phase

Background research was conducted into the Kerberos authentication protocol, specifically the TGS-REQ/TGS-REP exchange, SPN registration mechanics, and the role of encryption type negotiation. Published Microsoft security guidance, MITRE ATT&CK technique T1558.003, and CIS Benchmark recommendations for Active Directory were reviewed.

5.2 Lab Build Phase

An isolated lab was constructed following the documented procedures in ad_lab/AD_Lab_Setup.md:

  1. Configure VM network as Host-Only (no internet routing)
  2. Install Windows Server 2022 and promote to Domain Controller for lab.local
  3. Create OU structure and synthetic service accounts
  4. Register SPNs on the synthetic vulnerable account (svc-sqltest)
  5. Join CLIENT01 to the domain
  6. Take snapshots to preserve the baseline (pre-hardening) state

5.3 Baseline Assessment Phase

Using the Flask application's Risk Assessment module, the pre-hardening lab state was evaluated against the documented risk factors. The baseline expected findings include:

  • RC4 encryption allowed on service accounts → Critical
  • No Advanced Audit Policy for Kerberos → High
  • Static password on SPN account (no gMSA) → High
  • PowerShell logging not configured → Medium

5.4 Hardening Phase

Defensive controls were applied in the order documented in hardening/Security_Hardening_Baseline.md: AES enforcement, gMSA deployment, audit policy, PowerShell logging, Protected Users group, and Fine-Grained PSO. GPO backups were taken before and after each change.

5.5 Verification Phase

Each control was verified using the PowerShell commands listed in the Hardening Verification Matrix. Post-hardening audit of Event ID 4769 encryption type fields was performed to confirm RC4 tickets were no longer being issued.

Section 10

Limitations

  • Isolated lab only: Findings are based on a synthetic environment; enterprise behaviour may differ due to legacy compatibility requirements, domain trust relationships, or existing PSO conflicts.
  • No real ticket cracking performed: The project documents the vulnerability theoretically and defensively; no password cracking tools are executed against any accounts.
  • Evaluation OS licences: Windows Server 2022 and Windows 10/11 evaluation editions have a 180-day limit; the lab must be rebuilt periodically.
  • Static application data: The Flask application uses in-memory data structures; a production version would require a database and authentication layer.
  • No SIEM integration: Log correlation is documented conceptually; actual SIEM alerting was not configured in this phase.
  • gMSA limitations: gMSA requires all hosts using the account to be running supported OS versions; legacy applications may require special compatibility handling.
Section 11

Conclusion

Kerberoasting remains one of the most prevalent Active Directory attack techniques because it exploits a design characteristic of the Kerberos protocol and requires no special privileges. However, it is also one of the most preventable through a combination of well-understood defensive controls.

This project demonstrates that the primary attack surface — RC4-encrypted TGS tickets for accounts with static passwords — can be eliminated entirely through:

  • AES-only Kerberos enforcement via GPO, making offline cracking computationally infeasible
  • Group Managed Service Accounts, eliminating human-set passwords on SPN accounts entirely
  • Advanced Audit Policies on Event ID 4769, enabling detection of mass enumeration
  • PowerShell Script Block Logging, capturing tool-based Kerberoasting attempts
  • Least-privilege and Protected Users, limiting blast radius if any account is compromised

The companion Flask application provides an educational platform for scoring defensive posture and understanding risk scenarios, suitable for security awareness training, lab demonstration, and academic portfolio submission.
